title: Thermomechanics of dense granular materials: a particle-scale perspective
abstract: The paper presents a broad thermomechanic framework for the isothermal rate-independent constitutive behavior of dense granular materials. The essential quantities in this framework are directly measurable in discrete element (DEM) simulations: free energy, dissipation, stress, and strain. The paper proposes that energy and dissipation are governed by two sets of internal variables: fabric variables that control the reversible stiffness and structure variables associated with internal sliding. The relevant fabric variables are identified and measured with simulations. Two hypotheses are considered for the structure variables: the macro-scale irreversible strain and an aggregate measure of the micro-scale frictional forces among sliding contacts. Both hypotheses are tested with simulations, which allow direct calculation of the internal variables. The paper then demonstrates the manner in which the measured variables are applied in incremental constitutive models. Among other findings are the following. (1) Dissipation from contact sliding is pervasive and occurs in all directions of incremental loading. (2) Contact motions are not reversed by a reversal of the strain direction, and contacts continue to slide when loading is reversed. (3) The free energy can not be assumed smoothly differentiable; instead, Gâteaux derivatives must be used with irreversible effects. (4) Basic assumptions of elastoplasticity are contravened: no region of purely reversible strain exists, no uniform yield direction exists, no uniform flow direction exists, and irreversible strain is not proportional to the projected total strain. A three-mechanism elastoplasticity model, however, closely fit the DEM results, and methods are demonstrated for quantifying the model. The results emphasize that advanced constitutive models are needed for capturing the general incremental behavior of granular materials.
summary: This paper establishes a rigorous thermomechanical framework for understanding how dense granular materials behave under stress. It shows that standard assumptions from continuum mechanics break down due to pervasive energy dissipation during contact sliding. The work emphasizes the need for advanced constitutive models that accurately capture the complex, non-smooth nature of granular material response.
main_problem: Developing a comprehensive thermomechanical framework to describe the isothermal, rate-independent constitutive behavior of dense granular materials.
main_result: The paper demonstrates that basic elastoplastic assumptions fail for granular materials, necessitating advanced constitutive models that account for pervasive dissipation and non-smooth energy landscapes.
method: The authors utilize a combination of continuum mechanics theory, energy rate balance equations, and direct measurement techniques derived from Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations.
model_or_system: The system is dense granular material, modeled using a thermomechanical framework that incorporates internal variables for fabric (reversible stiffness) and structure (dissipation). The analysis is based on energy rate balance equations derived from the Helmholtz free energy density.
key_observables: Free energy ($\psi$), dissipation rate, stress ($ oldsymbol{\sigma}$), and strain ($ oldsymbol{\varepsilon}$), which are directly measurable in DEM simulations.
important_parameters: Isothermal conditions, rate-independence, and the nature of internal variables (fabric and structure).
main_assumptions: The framework assumes rate-independence and isothermal conditions, but acknowledges that the free energy may not be smoothly differentiable, requiring the use of Gâteaux derivatives.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the energy rate balance, proposing internal variable sets for fabric and structure, testing these variables against DEM results, and finally comparing the findings against standard elastoplastic assumptions.
why_interesting: While focused on classical mechanics, the rigorous treatment of non-equilibrium energy dissipation, path dependence, and the failure of simple constitutive assumptions mirrors challenges in modeling non-equilibrium quantum systems or complex many-body dynamics.
